claims.claim: Le Guin opens Steering the Craft by stating that the sound of the language is where it all begins.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised edition), chapter 1, published at Literary Hub
claims.quote: The sound of the language is where it all begins

claims.claim: Le Guin gives as the test of a sentence whether it sounds right.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised edition), chapter 1, at Literary Hub
claims.quote: The test of a sentence is, Does it sound right?

claims.claim: Le Guin states that the chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next sentence, so as to keep the story going.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised edition), chapter 1, at Literary Hub
claims.quote: The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead

claims.claim: Le Guin says of her Hurston and Molly Gloss examples that the vocabulary is simple and familiar and that it is above all the rhythm that is powerful and effective.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised edition), chapter 1, at Literary Hub
claims.quote: the vocabulary is simple and familiar

claims.claim: Le Guin describes Molly Gloss's prose as quiet and subtle, its power and beauty coming from the perfect placement and timing of the words.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised edition), chapter 1, at Literary Hub
claims.quote: the perfect placement and timing of the words

claims.claim: Le Guin poses as an open question for discussion whether a novelist who visibly strives for poetical prose using unusual or archaic words intensifies what is being said or distracts from it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised edition), chapter 1, at Literary Hub
claims.quote: using unusual or archaic words

claims.claim: Stephanie Burt distinguishes Earthsea from most fantasy by its clear, patient prose.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt, review of John Plotz's Ursula Le Guin's Earthsea, Strange Horizons, 6 November 2023
claims.quote: in its clear, patient prose

claims.claim: John Plotz, quoted by Stephanie Burt, calls Le Guin's prose the antithesis of the well-rendered verisimilitude of a high-end video game.
claims.source: John Plotz, Ursula Le Guin's Earthsea, p. 48, quoted in Stephanie Burt, Strange Horizons, 6 November 2023
claims.quote: the antithesis of the well-rendered verisimilitude of a high-end video game

claims.claim: Stephanie Burt reports that Le Guin's clear, spare prose reminds John Plotz of Willa Cather's, and says she agrees.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt, Strange Horizons, 6 November 2023
claims.quote: Her clear, spare prose reminds Plotz

claims.claim: The Ursula K. Le Guin Foundation records that From Elfland to Poughkeepsie was a speech given at the Second Annual Science Fiction Writers' Workshop in 1972 and first published by Pendragon Press in 1973 in a limited run of 776 copies, with reprints of 1006 copies in December 1975 and 2000 copies in April 1978.
claims.source: The Ursula K. Le Guin Foundation, ursulakleguin.com bibliography page
claims.quote: a limited run of 776 copies

claims.claim: Erin Ramsay writes that the mythic and fundamental register of A Wizard of Earthsea gives way to the realistic and mundane in The Tombs of Atuan.
claims.source: Erin Ramsay, 'Earthsea: A Sharpening of Scale', The Lighthouse (Substack), 16 April 2024
claims.quote: The mythic and fundamental in A Wizard of Earthsea gives way

claims.claim: Philip Chase reports that Le Guin's essay holds that good fantasy prose does not have to be archaic and does not even have to be elevated, but must not be journalistic.
claims.source: Philip Chase, 'What is good fantasy prose?' (video), 16 November 2021
claims.quote: good fantasy pros does not have to be archaic

claims.claim: Philip Chase disagrees with Le Guin's use of E. R. Eddison as an example of exemplary fantasy prose, saying he would not hold it up for fantasy writers today.
claims.source: Philip Chase, 'What is good fantasy prose?' (video), 16 November 2021
claims.quote: this is an example that i personally would disagree with today

claims.claim: Philip Chase argues that the tightrope Le Guin describes between over-archaic and journalistic prose moves with time, so that Eddison's prose reads as more overdone now than it did in 1973.
claims.source: Philip Chase, 'What is good fantasy prose?' (video), 16 November 2021
claims.quote: the tightrope might actually move with time

claims.claim: The reviewer on A Novel Review calls Le Guin's Earthsea prose really simple prose that ferries the reader along.
claims.source: A Novel Review - Book Podcast (video), 11 August 2025
claims.quote: It's really simple prose, but very ferries you along

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Kate Nepveu from 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings', describes the rhythm shaping Tolkien's narrative as very strong and very simple, as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (Meditations on Middle-earth, 2001; reprinted in The Wave in the Mind), quoted in Kate Nepveu, LiveJournal, 4 June 2006
claims.quote: very strong and very simple, as simple as a rhythm can be

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Kate Nepveu, glosses that two-beat rhythm as stress and release, inbreath and outbreath, a heartbeat, a walking gait.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings', quoted in Kate Nepveu, LiveJournal, 4 June 2006
claims.quote: Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath. A heartbeat.

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Kate Nepveu, says of the closing lines of Tolkien's barrow-downs chapter that the tone is quiet, the language simple, and the emotions evoked quiet, simple and common.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings', quoted in Kate Nepveu, LiveJournal, 4 June 2006
claims.quote: Yet the tone is quiet, the language simple

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Erik Mueller-Harder, wrote that even when Tolkien's sentences are long their flow is perfectly clear and follows the breath, punctuation comes just where you need to pause, and the cadences are graceful and inevitable.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), quoted in Erik D. Mueller-Harder, Vermont Softworks, 28 September 2023
claims.quote: Even when the sentences are long, their flow is perfectly clear

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Erik Mueller-Harder, wrote that Tolkien must have heard what he wrote.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), quoted in Erik D. Mueller-Harder, Vermont Softworks, 28 September 2023
claims.quote: Tolkien must have heard what he wrote

claims.claim: Le Guin writes that a plain language is the noblest of all.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973), quoted in Barbara J. Bucknall, Ursula K. Le Guin (1981)
claims.quote: A plain language is the noblest of all

claims.claim: Le Guin adds that plain language is also the most difficult.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973), quoted in Bucknall (1981)
claims.quote: It is also the most difficult

claims.claim: Le Guin writes that clarity and simplicity are permanent virtues in a narrative.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973), quoted in Bucknall (1981)
claims.quote: Clarity and simplicity are permanent virtues in a narrative

claims.claim: Dirda says the sentences of A Wizard of Earthsea are formal, clear, and exact.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, Ursula K. Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea teacher's guide, NEA Big Read (National Endowment for the Arts, 2008)
claims.quote: The sentences are formal, clear, and exact

claims.claim: Dirda says those sentences carry the musical cadence of an oral storyteller.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, NEA Big Read teacher's guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (2008)
claims.quote: with the musical cadence of an oral storyteller

claims.claim: Dirda says Le Guin gives music and richness to her prose through the rhythm of her sentences.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, NEA Big Read teacher's guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (2008)
claims.quote: music and richness to her prose through the rhythm

claims.claim: Dirda says heroic or high fantasy demands a slightly formal, elevated style.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, NEA Big Read teacher's guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (2008)
claims.quote: a slightly formal, elevated style

claims.claim: Burt calls the prose of Earthsea clear and patient.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt, review of John Plotz's Ursula Le Guin's Earthsea, Strange Horizons, 6 November 2023
claims.quote: its clear, patient prose

claims.claim: Plotz calls Le Guin's prose the antithesis of the well-rendered verisimilitude of a high-end video game.
claims.source: John Plotz, Ursula Le Guin's Earthsea (Oxford Univ. Press, 2023), p. 48, quoted in Stephanie Burt, Strange Horizons, 6 November 2023
claims.quote: the antithesis of the well-rendered verisimilitude

claims.claim: Burt reports that Le Guin's clear, spare prose reminds Plotz of Willa Cather's.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt, review of Plotz, Strange Horizons, 6 November 2023
claims.quote: Her clear, spare prose reminds Plotz

claims.claim: Burt says Le Guin works at the level of the sentence, letting readers fill in the details of her strongly outlined world.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt, review of Plotz, Strange Horizons, 6 November 2023
claims.quote: letting us fill in the details of her strongly outlined world

claims.claim: Le Guin says names come first with her.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 2015 interview with John Plotz, transcribed in Public Books, 21 February 2024
claims.quote: Names come first with me

claims.claim: Plotz quotes Le Guin's essay as saying fantasy offers only a construct built in a void with every joint and seam and nail exposed.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973), quoted by John Plotz in Public Books, 21 February 2024
claims.quote: a construct built in a void

claims.claim: Le Guin states that a plain language is the noblest of all.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (speech 1972; Pendragon Press booklet 1973; in The Language of the Night, 1979)
claims.quote: A plain language is the noblest of all.

claims.claim: Le Guin calls clarity and simplicity permanent virtues in a narrative.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (speech 1972; booklet 1973; in The Language of the Night, 1979)
claims.quote: Clarity and simplicity are permanent virtues in a narrative.

claims.claim: Le Guin says that plain language is also the most difficult kind to write.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: It is also the most difficult.

claims.claim: Le Guin says the outstanding virtue of Tolkien's plain English is its flexibility, ranging easily from the commonplace to the stately.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately

claims.claim: Le Guin distinguishes a fake plainness that is not really simple but flat from genuine plain style.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: It is not really simple, but flat.

claims.claim: Le Guin faults the flat fantasy style because its rocks, wind and trees are not there and not felt.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: the rocks, the wind, the trees are not there

claims.claim: Le Guin calls the archaic manner a trap into which almost all very young fantasy writers walk, and says she did herself.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: a trap into which almost all very young fantasy writers walk

claims.claim: Le Guin says a secondary world is a construct built in a void with every joint and seam and nail exposed, because there is no borrowed reality to hide behind.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: with every joint and seam and nail exposed

claims.claim: Le Guin ends her account of the secondary world with the sentence that every word counts.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: And every word counts.

claims.claim: Le Guin defines the musical dimension of prose as the sound of the words, the movement of the syntax and the rhythm of the sentences.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: the movement of the syntax, and the rhythm of the sentences

claims.claim: Le Guin says Jack Vance's achieved style contains no archaisms at all.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: it contains no archaisms at all

claims.claim: Le Guin says Tolkien's references to places, people and events outside the immediate story give the reader a conviction of the reality of the immediate scene.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Plausibility in Fantasy: an open letter to Alexei Mutovkin" (2005), ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: a conviction of the reality of the immediate scene

claims.claim: Le Guin says exact and vivid words make an exact and vivid world.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Plausibility in Fantasy: an open letter to Alexei Mutovkin" (2005)
claims.quote: Exact and vivid words make an exact and vivid world.

claims.claim: Le Guin says she has often mentioned events and places in her fantasies that she did not yet know anything about, which were merely words when she wrote them.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Plausibility in Fantasy: an open letter to Alexei Mutovkin" (2005)
claims.quote: These were, when I wrote them, merely words

claims.claim: Le Guin says that a fantasy world resembling preindustrial mediaeval Europe is not thereby justified in having no economics and no social justice.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Some Assumptions about Fantasy", speech at the Children's Literature Breakfast, BookExpo America, Chicago, 4 June 2004
claims.quote: no economics and no social justice

claims.claim: Le Guin says she feels like setting off fireworks whenever she finds a fantasy set in a genuinely imagined society and culture.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Some Assumptions about Fantasy" (BookExpo America, 4 June 2004)
claims.quote: set in a genuinely imagined society and culture

claims.claim: Le Guin says that in describing an invented world the leaving-out is half the art, and the reader fills the white spaces.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin interviewed by John Plotz, Public Books, 15 June 2015
claims.quote: the leaving-out is half the art

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by a blogger, says that even when Tolkien's sentences are long their flow is clear and punctuation comes just where you need to pause.
claims.source: Erik D. Mueller-Harder, Vermont Softworks blog, 28 September 2023, quoting Le Guin, "Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings" (Meditations on Middle-earth, 2001)
claims.quote: punctuation comes just where you need to pause

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by a blogger, calls the cadences of Tolkien's prose graceful and inevitable.
claims.source: Erik D. Mueller-Harder, Vermont Softworks blog, 28 September 2023, quoting Le Guin, "Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings" (2001)
claims.quote: the cadences are graceful and inevitable

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by a blogger, concludes that Tolkien must have heard what he wrote.
claims.source: Erik D. Mueller-Harder, Vermont Softworks blog, 28 September 2023, quoting Le Guin, "Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings" (2001)
claims.quote: Tolkien must have heard what he wrote

claims.claim: Le Guin says part of doing as little as possible is leaving a lot of it up to the reader.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin interviewed by Paul Morton, The Millions, 31 January 2013
claims.quote: leaving a lot of it up to the reader

claims.claim: Le Guin says her writing has tended to become shorter and more allusive than it used to be.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin interviewed by Paul Morton, The Millions, 31 January 2013
claims.quote: shorter and more allusive than it used to be

claims.claim: Le Guin gives pronunciation guidelines for her invented names because how a name is said affects the sound and rhythm of a sentence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Ursula on Ursula" (pronunciation guide and reader notes), ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: this does affect the sound and rhythm of a sentence
